title: The order was clear.
paragraphs: The order was clear.
Kill the sons. Let the daughters live.
And in a world where power spoke with the voice of law, two women stood in the shadows and refused to become servants of death.
Shiphrah. Puah.
Read that again.
They were not generals. Not queens. Not rulers seated on thrones. They were midwives—ordinary women placed in an unbearable moment, where obedience to man demanded rebellion against God.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…

Exodus does not first spotlight Pharaoh’s strength. It exposes his fear. A king with armies was trembling over babies. A ruler with authority was threatened by life itself. That is what darkness always does. It fears what God is bringing forth.
And the midwives saw the line. They feared God more than they feared the crown.
That one decision changed everything.

Not because they were sinless.
Not because they were powerful.
Not because human courage can save the world.
But because the fear of the Lord made them refuse partnership with evil.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior, this is where the story pierces deeper than history. It reaches into you.

Because every generation faces this question:
Who will you obey when human authority demands what God forbids?

And the pressure is real.
Sometimes authority wears a crown.
Sometimes it wears culture.
Sometimes it wears policy, popularity, threat, or applause.
Sometimes it sounds reasonable.
Sometimes it even sounds necessary.
But when authority commands death, silence, compromise, or the violation of what God has made sacred, obedience to God becomes costly.
And that cost reveals the heart.
If this found you, it’s not by accident.

You may never stand in Pharaoh’s court, but you will stand in moments where righteousness costs you something. And in those moments, courage alone is not enough. You need more than principle. You need truth rooted in the fear of God. Explore more here:
But don’t miss the deeper wound in the story.

Pharaoh’s command was not just political evil. It was the fruit of sin. Human rebellion against God always produces death. From Eden onward, sin has tried to destroy what God creates. It corrupts hearts, twists authority, and normalizes cruelty.
And that means this is not only Pharaoh’s problem.
It is ours.

Apart from Christ, the human heart does not merely witness evil—it participates in it. Maybe not with a royal decree. Maybe not with public violence. But with pride. With fear. With selfishness. With silence. With compromise.
That is why the message cannot stop at “be brave like the midwives.”
Moral examples cannot redeem sinners.

You need more than a model.
You need a Savior.
And His name is Jesus Christ.

Jesus entered a world ruled by corrupt authority. He was hated, rejected, and condemned under human systems drenched in injustice. Yet unlike Pharaoh, He did not take life—He laid down His own. At the cross, the full horror of sin was exposed, and the full mercy of God was revealed. The judgment we deserved fell on Him. The grace we could never earn was opened through Him.

This is the Gospel:
You are a sinner.
Your sin leads to death.
No work, no courage, no morality can cleanse you.
But Jesus lived the righteous life you could not live, died the death you deserved, and rose again in victory.
Turn from sin. Repent. Put your faith in Christ alone.
Grace is not earned. Redemption is received.
That is the difference between religion and rescue.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…

The same God who honored the midwives still honors those who fear Him above men. Not always with ease. Not always with immediate vindication. But always with His presence, and ultimately with eternal reward in Christ. He sees quiet faithfulness. He sees trembling obedience. He sees the hidden stand no one applauds.
Read that again.
He sees.
And maybe that is where you are today—caught between pressure and conviction, between safety and obedience, between what is demanded and what is right.

Then hear this clearly:
Do not bow to darkness to preserve yourself.
Run to Jesus to truly live.

So now the question turns back to you.

Where have you been tempted to obey fear instead of God?
What “Pharaoh” has been trying to name what God has already made holy?
And what would change if you feared the Lord more than man?
